In my first few years trading, I saved +10,000s of charts into a playbook and studied the greatest traders I could find until the patterns almost became subconscious.

Funny enough, over the last year I’ve barely looked back at those old charts. And it wasn't because they stopped being valuable, but because after +6 years of staring at charts every day, eventually pattern recognition starts becoming second nature.

I don’t think newer traders realize how powerful building a playbook is in the beginning.

You’re basically training your eyes with thousands of reps before real $$ is on the line. At some point you may outgrow needing to study it constantly, but I genuinely think it was one of the best foundations I built early on.

Fascinating looking back at it now… curious if other experienced traders eventually stopped reviewing old charts as much too?

If you want evidence this year has been tricky this is it.

When I'm trying to figure out whether institutions are accumulating a stock, I look for evidence in price + volume.

I'm looking for these 4 footprints:

1) Higher lows = buyers are stepping up.
2) Stage 1 → Stage 2 transition = the character of the stock may be changing.
3) Volume drying up on pullbacks into the 9/21EMA = sellers aren't showing much urgency.
4) Relative strength vs. the market + its peers = capital is flowing somewhere for a reason.

None of these things mean a stock "has" to go higher.

But when I start seeing multiple layers of probability stack up, I start to watch. That's basically my entire process:

Find the footprints + isolate the leaders + wait for tight risk + sit in stage 2 stocks = butter:)

When I first started out, I watched the screen and traded every single second the market was open. There was absolutely zero control. 

I felt like I had to be in everything, all at the same time. I was constantly running from one stock to another just because the new one looked a little better or was moving a little faster. It was pure exhaustion.

After a few years of getting chopped up, everything shifted:

Now, I trade less and watch more. 

I can sit there and see 20 great ideas cross my desk, and I will only execute on 5 of them. 

That is the simple math of a professional trader. 

You do not need more trades to make more money. You need more patience, tighter execution, and the discipline to let good setups pass so you can load the boat on the elite ones.

@stevenpetnia Both, but location/environment comes first, and price action decides the trigger.

If a leader is gapping through a major daily/weekly pivot with momentum, I may use a 5/15/30min ORB because I’m willing to pay up for confirmation... if it flushes into the 9/21EMA, prior breakout, PLOD, etc., I’d rather wait for buyers to prove themselves through a VWAP reclaim, 15/30min pivot, or 6/20 cross.

I’m basically asking: where is my higher TF inflection point, are buyers actually defending it, and what lower TF trigger gives me the tightest risk against LOD?

Same setups, different entry tactics depending on how price arrives at the level + the environment I’m trading in.

My entries work backward:

Environment first...
1) higher TF pivot (daily/weekly)
2) observe reaction on lower TF (30/65min)
3) lower TF confirmation (5/15/30min)
4) define risk
5) execute

The 15/30min chart means NOTHING to me without the daily + weekly location first.

Risk-to-reward (R:R) tells you how much you could make relative to what you’re risking.

If you risk $100 to potentially make $300, that’s a 3:1 R:R—or a 3R target.

But a high R:R means nothing without a realistic probability of reaching it. Trading expectancy comes from balancing win rate, average winner and average loser—not simply chasing the tightest stop and biggest target.

Need to be said, but if your question takes 5 seconds to Google, Google it first.

Before asking someone for their time, research the topic, try it yourself, figure out exactly where you’re stuck, then ask about THAT.

Instead of “How do I become profitable?” ask, “What mistake kept you unprofitable the longest, and what specifically changed?”

Good questions get good answers... learn that skill early, and you can save yourself years of unnecessary trial + error.
